bib.title: NumPy Basics: Arrays and Vectorized Computation (Chapter 4, Python for Data Analysis, 2nd ed.)

question: How do NumPy ndarrays, ufuncs and array-oriented idioms replace Python loops for fast numerical data work?
contributions: Introduces ndarray creation, dtypes, vectorized arithmetic, indexing (basic, boolean, fancy), transposition, ufuncs, array-oriented programming (where, reductions, sort, set ops), file I/O, linear algebra, random numbers and a random-walk example.

results.claim: Multiplying a 1,000,000-element NumPy int array by 2, 10 times, took 72.4 ms wall time versus 1.05 s for the equivalent Python list comprehension.
results.setup: np.arange(1000000) vs list(range(1000000)); IPython %time, single run, 10 loops of x*2; machine and NumPy version not stated
results.note: Ratio ~14.5x is derived (1.05 s / 72.4 ms), not printed; the text states 'generally 10 to 100 times faster (or more)'. Sys+user CPU: 70 ms vs 1.05 s.

results.claim: The author states NumPy algorithms are generally 10 to 100 times faster and use less memory than pure Python.
results.setup: General statement following the million-element example; no further data
results.quote:
NumPy-based algorithms are generally 10 to 100 times faster (or more) than their
pure Python counterparts and use significantly less memory.

results.claim: Vectorized array operations are often one or two (or more) orders of magnitude faster than pure Python equivalents.
results.setup: Section 4.3 definition of vectorization; no data
results.quote:
vectorized array operations will often be one or two (or more) orders
of magnitude faster than their pure Python equivalents

results.claim: Generating 1,000,000 normal samples with np.random.normal took 61.7 ms versus 1.77 s for a list comprehension over random.normalvariate.
results.setup: N = 1000000; %timeit; NumPy size=N call vs [normalvariate(0, 1) for _ in range(N)]; machine not stated
results.quote: 61.7 ms +- 1.32 ms per loop (mean +- std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
results.note: Ratio ~28.7x derived (1.77 s / 61.7 ms); text says 'well over an order of magnitude faster'.

results.claim: Slices are views, not copies: writing to arr_slice changes arr.
results.quote: array slices are views on the original array.

results.claim: Boolean indexing always returns a copy, as does fancy indexing; slicing returns a view.
results.quote:
Selecting data from an array by boolean indexing always creates a copy of the data,
even if the returned array is unchanged.

results.claim: Fancy indexing with multiple index arrays selects element tuples and returns a 1-D array: arr[[1,5,7,2],[0,3,1,2]] gives [4,23,29,10].
results.quote:
Regardless of
how many dimensions the array has (here, only 2), the result of fancy indexing is
always one-dimensional.

results.claim: Boolean selection does not fail on a mask of the wrong length.
results.quote:
Boolean selection will not fail if the boolean array is not the correct
length, so I recommend care when using this feature.

results.claim: Python and/or keywords do not work with boolean arrays; use & and |.
results.quote: The Python keywords and and or do not work with boolean arrays.

results.claim: In a 5000 x 1000-step +-1 random walk simulation, 3410 walks hit +-30, with mean first crossing time 498.89 steps.
results.setup: nwalks=5000, nsteps=1000, unseeded np.random.randint draws; single run
results.quote:
hits30.sum() # Number that hit 30 or -30
Out[268]: 3410
results.note: Mean crossing time printed as 498.88973607038122; walks.max() 138, walks.min() -133. Unseeded, so not reproducible exactly.

results.claim: A single 1000-step walk had min -3, max 31 and first crossing of |10| at step 37.
argmax on a boolean array finds the first True but always scans the whole array.
results.quote:
using argmax here is not always efficient because it always makes a full scan
of the array

results.claim: np.empty may return uninitialized garbage values rather than zeros.
results.quote:
It’s not safe to assume that np.empty will return an array of all
zeros.
results.note: Source uses a curly apostrophe in It's.

limits: Timings are single IPython sessions with no hardware, NumPy or Python version stated.
Edition predates modern NumPy: np.random.RandomState/seed (now Generator), np.in1d (now np.isin), np.string_ and float128 names have changed or been deprecated.
Broadcasting, reshape, indirect sorts deferred to Appendix A.
Output shows dtype=bool arrays and 'array(...)' reprs from old NumPy; int64 default is platform-dependent.
practices: Use import numpy as np and avoid from numpy import *, because names like min and max clash with built-ins (p.88).
Replace for loops with array expressions (vectorization) for 10-100x speed (p.87, p.108).
Call .copy() explicitly when you want a copy of a slice, since slices are views (p.95).
Do not assume np.empty returns zeros (p.90).
Be cautious with fixed-size numpy string_ dtype, which may truncate silently; prefer pandas for non-numeric data (p.92).
Use & and | with parentheses, not and/or, to combine boolean masks (p.101).
Check boolean mask length yourself because wrong lengths do not raise (p.100).
Use np.where(cond, x, y) instead of a list comprehension with a conditional for vectorized if/else (p.110).
Use (arr > 0).sum() to count True values since booleans coerce to 1/0 (p.113).
Use x @ y or np.dot for matrix product; * is element-wise (p.116).
Use np.random.RandomState(seed) for an isolated generator instead of the global seed (p.119).
For rectangular fancy selection use arr[rows][:, cols] (p.103).
Use np.save/np.load for binary arrays and savez_compressed when data compress well (p.115-116).
